examples.before:
.troupe/troupe.yml:
# two agents share one settings file
a: file:shared.yml
b: file:shared.yml  # same include

.troupe/shared.yml:
model: opus  # shared
temperature: 0.2
examples.input: `config history` (first run on the starting files)

results.1: All six arms: exit 0; four import entries (a.model=opus, a.temperature=0.2, b.model=opus, b.temperature=0.2), each with actor kind "unknown" and via "import".

Three arms: exit 0, no output; .troupe/shared.yml now reads:
model: sonnet # shared
temperature: 0.2
(the two spaces before the comment became one). Three arms: exit 3, no file changed, each with a different message: "troupe: a.model: the edited files would not read back as intended; not writing" / "troupe: a.model: cannot write this change byte-surgically; no file changed" / "troupe: a.model: write-back would disturb b.model".
Three arms (the ones that wrote): prints `sonnet`, so b changed even though only a was set. Three arms (the ones that refused): prints `opus`.
All six arms: exit 0; every value is labelled `# from .troupe/shared.yml`. Three arms show model: sonnet for both a and b; three arms show model: opus for both.

Three arms that wrote: the two import entries, then `{"seq": 6, "op": "set", "path": "b.model", "old": "opus", "new": "sonnet", "actor": {"kind": "human", "id": "owner"}, "via": "cli", ...}`, so b's history records the change the owner made through a. Three arms that refused: only the two import entries.

context.in_practice: There is only one route, and its six arms split evenly. In half of them, setting one agent's value in a shared include also changes it for every agent using that file, records the change in each agent's history, and changes the comment spacing on the edited line. In the other half, the set is refused with exit 3 and the files stay untouched, so you have to edit the shared file yourself (or split it) to change the value.
context.stakes: When two agents load the same included settings file, changing one agent's value either silently changes the other agent's value too, or is refused. Every implementation reads current values from the files, so the outcome depends on how each one handles that shared file.
context.tradeoff: Route 1 always treats the files as the truth, but depending on the arm a set on a shared include either changes every agent that uses it or is refused outright.

plan_why: Two keys include the same file, so a set through one also changes the other in the file; get, show and history then show whether values are read from the files (b.model follows the edit) or from a per-path event projection (b.model stays stale, or turns up later as a reconcile event)
routes: Files on disk are authoritative; show and set read the files; the store is change history only
